soil-found-077.q: What are the two main historical branches of soil science, and how do they differ?
soil-found-077.a: Pedology studies soil in its natural setting, while edaphology studies soil in relation to the uses that depend on it.

soil-found-097.q: In a typical soil, how is the volume shared between solids and pores?
soil-found-097.a: About half is solids (45% mineral and 5% organic matter) and half is pores, split equally between water and gas.

soil-found-091.q: Before Fallou and Dokuchaev, how was soil generally seen?
soil-found-091.a: As a product of chemical transformations of rocks: a dead substrate from which plants draw nutrients.

soil-found-096.q: Why do classifications not rest on soil genesis alone?
soil-found-096.a: Soil-forming processes are seldom observed and change over time, so genesis aids classification but cannot be its only basis.

soil-found-089.q: Why do tropical soils turn rusty red instead of showing podzolized layers?
soil-found-089.a: Fast decomposition leaves little fulvic acid to leach metals, so mobile magnesium, iron and aluminium precipitate as oxide minerals.

soil-found-098.q: What did van Helmont conclude from his willow experiment?
soil-found-098.a: Seeing the tree gain more weight than the soil lost, he concluded the willow was made of water, which was only partly correct.

soil-found-052.a: Weathering happens in place, while erosion carries rock and mineral material away by water, ice, wind, waves or gravity.

soil-found-063.q: True or false: rainwater can dissolve quartz.
soil-found-063.a: True: given enough time even quartz dissolves, going into solution as silicic acid.

soil-found-048.q: Why is frost wedging unlikely to dominate in the tropics or in arid climates?
soil-found-048.a: It needs daily freeze–thaw cycles of nearly saturated rock, conditions those climates do not supply.

soil-found-056.q: How does pressure release make rock break into sheets?
soil-found-056.a: When erosion strips the rock above, the outer parts of deep-formed rock expand, opening fractures parallel to the surface along which sheets break away.

soil-found-037.q: Why does a quartz-rich rock count as mature?
soil-found-037.a: Quartz is the primary mineral that survives heavy weathering, so its abundance shows long weathering.

soil-found-051.q: Unlike soil structure, can farming change a soil's texture?
soil-found-051.a: No: texture is fixed by the soil's mineral component and does not change with farming.

soil-found-043.q: Why do igneous minerals weather in roughly the order they formed?
soil-found-043.a: Acid hydrolysis breaks the weakest cation–oxygen bonds first, following Bowen's reaction series.

soil-found-038.q: Why is a pH of 3.5 so much more acidic than a pH of 9.5?
soil-found-038.a: The pH scale is logarithmic, so a solution at pH 3.5 has one million times more hydronium ions than one at pH 9.5.

soil-found-024.q: Why does a clay- and humus-rich soil need more lime to change its pH?
soil-found-024.a: Its colloids buffer strongly, and lime must also neutralise the exchangeable acidity they hold, or the stored cations restore the original pH.

soil-found-016.q: What does litmus paper show when dipped in a soil–water mix?
soil-found-016.a: It turns red if the soil is acidic and blue if it is basic.

soil-found-022.q: Why can roots in strongly acidic soil suffer moisture stress even when the soil is fairly moist?
soil-found-022.a: Aluminium toxicity limits root growth so much that the plant cannot take up enough water.

soil-found-026.q: In the Munsell notation 10R 4/8, what do the three parts stand for?
soil-found-026.a: 10R is the hue, 4 the value and 8 the chroma, written as hue, then value/chroma.

soil-form-100.q: How does saprolite differ from saprock?
soil-form-100.a: Saprolite is weathered rock, oxidised in its upper part and partly weathered below, while saprock is fractured bedrock weathered only along its fractures.

soil-form-087.q: Which plant nutrients does rock not supply to soil?
soil-form-087.a: Nitrogen, hydrogen and carbon; rock is the source of every other plant nutrient.

soil-form-113.q: What is the soil of the Loess Plateau known for?
soil-form-113.a: It has been called the most highly erodible soil on Earth.

soil-form-108.q: How does residuum differ from saprolite?
soil-form-108.a: Saprolite keeps its bedrock's structural features, while residuum has lost them, being transformed further and shrunk in volume.

soil-form-095.q: Why do soils formed in lake deposits tend to have low permeability?
soil-form-095.a: Lacustrine material has a high clay content.

soil-form-092.q: What makes river meanders become better defined over time?
soil-form-092.a: Cut-bank erosion usually equals point-bar deposition, and point bars push flow into the opposite bank.

soil-form-021.q: How does eluviation differ from leaching?
soil-form-021.a: Eluviation moves mineral and organic colloids, while leaching is a distinct mechanism of soil formation.

soil-form-017.q: How do hardpans made by people differ in origin from natural ones?
soil-form-017.a: Natural pans form when deposits such as silica, iron oxides or calcium carbonate bind soil particles; man-made ones are compacted by repeated ploughing, heavy traffic or pollution.

soil-form-034.a: Illuviation moves material basically vertically within the soil, while alluviation is the horizontal transfer by running water.

soil-form-024.q: In a horizon label such as 2Bt2, what do the leading and trailing numbers mean?
soil-form-024.a: The prefix 2 marks a lithologic discontinuity, a change in parent material; the suffix 2 marks a subdivision of one horizon.

soil-form-014.q: What does a sequence like O, A1, A2, B2, 2A2, 2B21 reveal about a soil's history?
soil-form-014.a: A fully formed profile was buried by sediments that later formed a new profile; the buried one starts at 2A2.

soil-form-028.q: How can a fragipan be told apart from a duripan?
soil-form-028.a: Air-dry fragipan fragments slake in water, unlike duripans and petrocalcic horizons.

soil-form-020.q: Why can a claypan soil be waterlogged yet leave plants short of water?
soil-form-020.a: Most of the water it holds is unavailable because it evaporates and the pores are tiny, while its dense layer can perch a water table on top.

soil-form-030.q: What do the old terms pedocal and pedalfer distinguish?
soil-form-030.a: Marbut split soils into pedocals, with calcite building up as caliche in the B horizon, and pedalfers, rich in aluminium and iron.

soil-form-031.q: What does a cambic horizon become as a soil develops into an Alfisol?
soil-form-031.a: An argillic (Bt) horizon, which holds more clay than the cambic horizon.

soil-form-042.q: Which soil-forming factor is regarded as dominant?
soil-form-042.a: Climate: soils show the distinctive characteristics of the climate zones in which they form.

soil-form-044.q: How do animals that mix soil affect the horizons?
soil-form-044.a: Their mixing, sometimes called pedoturbation, tends to undo the processes that create distinct horizons.

soil-form-049.q: Why are crest soils on a catena drier than toeslope soils?
soil-form-049.a: Crests drain freely, while toeslopes are wetter, poorly drained and richer in clay and organic matter.

soil-form-055.q: What key assumption does a chronosequence make, and why is it debated?
soil-form-055.a: It assumes nothing but age differs between sites, which often cannot be tested.

soil-form-061.q: In Erhart's theory, what happens to soils during rhexistasy?
soil-form-061.a: A drier climate thins vegetation, physical weathering dominates, and intense rains erode soils into layers of sand and silt.

soil-form-064.q: Why does modern soil classification fit paleosols poorly?
soil-form-064.a: Geology, life and the atmosphere changed greatly over the record, and an alfisol, for example, could not exist before trees.

soil-form-073.q: Why can laterite be cut from the ground yet serve as durable building stone?
soil-form-073.a: It is mined below the water table while wet and soft; as it dries, iron compounds lock into a rigid lattice that resists the weather.

soil-form-067.q: How is ferrallitisation the reverse of podsolisation?
soil-form-067.a: In ferrallitisation silica is leached away and iron and aluminium sesquioxides remain; in podsolisation silica remains and iron and aluminium are removed.

soil-form-052.q: In biosorting, why do large stones end up at the base of the biomantle?
soil-form-052.a: Burrowers move only particles smaller than their burrows, so larger stones settle and form a stonelayer.

soil-form-062.q: How does soil memory in soils differ from memory in layered sediments?
soil-form-062.a: Soils store records palimpsest-wise, with features overprinting each other, while sediments store them book-wise, in datable order.

soil-phys-014.q: Why do geotechnical engineers separate silts from clays by plasticity rather than size?
soil-phys-014.a: Size does not fix mineral makeup, so engineers use plasticity measured with the Atterberg limits instead.

soil-phys-053.q: What makes loam the only distinctive class in the USDA texture triangle?
soil-phys-053.a: It is the only class not dominated by sand, silt or clay.

soil-phys-046.q: In the ribbon test, what does the length of the unbroken ribbon indicate?
soil-phys-046.a: How much clay the sample holds.

soil-phys-003.q: What is the difference between a ped and a clod?
soil-phys-003.a: A ped forms naturally as particles clump into aggregates, while a clod is a mass of soil made artificially, for example by cultivation.

soil-phys-019.q: Why can sieving alone not complete a soil's particle-size analysis?
soil-phys-019.a: Silt and clay below 60 μm need a second method, usually the hydrometer or pipette, on the material from the bottom sieve.

soil-phys-051.q: Why does laser diffraction usually size platy clay larger than sedimentation analysis does?
soil-phys-051.a: Its theories assume spherical particles, so a clay plate is sized by its cross-section.

soil-phys-021.q: In the USCS symbol CH, what do the two letters mean?
soil-phys-021.a: C names the main material, clay, and H means a high liquid limit.

soil-phys-017.q: How is cumulative percent passing found from cumulative percent retained?
soil-phys-017.a: It equals 100% minus the cumulative percent retained.

soil-phys-026.q: What do the liquidity and consistency indices always add up to?

soil-phys-024.q: Why does sodium make clay deflocculate?
soil-phys-024.a: Clay flocculates when the slightly positive edges of plates stick to the negative faces of others, and sodium displacing polyvalent cations weakens this.

soil-phys-039.q: Above what exchangeable sodium percentage does dispersion become highly likely?

soil-phys-011.q: Is every crusting soil also hardsetting?
soil-phys-011.a: No: a hardsetting horizon is thicker than a crust, often as thick as the cultivated layer or more.

soil-phys-057.q: When is a sand classed as well graded (SW) under the USCS?
soil-phys-057.a: When Cu ≥ 6 and 1 < Cc < 3; otherwise it is poorly graded (SP).

soil-phys-063.q: How do bulk density and porosity relate in a dry soil?
soil-phys-063.a: Inversely: the more pore space a soil has, the lower its bulk density.

soil-phys-069.q: Why is compaction harder to manage than salinization or erosion?
soil-phys-069.a: It is mainly a hidden, sub-surface problem, so special methods are needed to locate it.

soil-phys-073.q: Why does higher pore water pressure make soil weaker?
soil-phys-073.a: Strength comes mainly from friction proportional to normal stress, and effective stress is total stress minus pore water pressure.

soil-phys-116.q: Why does a saturated clay settle so much more slowly than a sand under load?
soil-phys-116.a: Clay's extremely low hydraulic conductivity lets water drain only slowly, while coarse soils drain readily and settle at once.

soil-phys-109.q: Why does a wet sandcastle stand but collapse when submerged?
soil-phys-109.a: Water above the water table is at negative pressure, pulling grains together so friction holds them; submerged, that pull is lost.

soil-phys-094.q: How does compaction reduce the nitrogen available to crops?
soil-phys-094.a: Poorer oxygen diffusion with wetter conditions boosts denitrification, raising N2O emissions and lowering crop nitrogen.

soil-phys-091.q: Why are fine-textured, wet soils most easily compacted?
soil-phys-091.a: Water films shield the contacts between particles, and clay-rich soils are more susceptible than coarse ones.

soil-phys-068.q: Why can clay be highly porous yet conduct water poorly?
soil-phys-068.a: It stores much water per volume but releases it slowly through narrow pore throats.

soil-phys-133.q: Why does pumping groundwater make the land surface sink?
soil-phys-133.a: Pumping changes the effective stress on compressible silt or clay layers, which consolidate, often irreversibly, and lose volume.
